name_en: Kolmogorov weak-type theorem for conjugate functions
source_attribution: Andrey Kolmogorov, 1925 (catalog metadata, matched at intake to Kolmogoroff 1925 Theorem I)
candidate_family_not_credited_as_stateme: There exists an absolute constant C such that for every summable periodic function f, its source-normalized almost-everywhere boundary conjugate g, and every positive finite threshold R, angular_measure({theta | |g(theta)| > R}) * R is at most C times the integral of |f| over one angular period.
target_disposition: independently review Kolmogoroff 1925 Theorem I, then elaborate the exact source-selected periodic weak-(1,1) proposition with checked representation and normalization bridges
statement_blocker: The primary theorem is pinpointed, but statement acceptance must still fix angular Lebesgue versus probability-normalized Haar measure, real or complex inputs, function versus L1-class binders and representative invariance, disk-boundary versus principal-value versus Fourier-multiplier construction of g, additive-constant/zero-mode normalization, the positive finite threshold type, strict versus non-strict level sets and inequalities, and ordered quantifier scope. Choosing these silently at intake would risk a broadened or substituted target.
domain_and_universes: Source domain: summable periodic scalar functions on the angular interval [-pi, pi], their disk harmonic conjugates and almost-everywhere boundary values, angular Lebesgue measure, and a real threshold. Lean carrier, scalar field, quotient representative policy, universes, and typeclass context remain to be fixed.
conclusion: Open as a canonical Lean target. The source candidate concludes an absolute-constant weak-(1,1) superlevel estimate for the periodic conjugate function.
degenerate_case_status: No formal case is excluded before the target is selected. Statement work must test zero and constant inputs, mean/zero-mode normalization, null-set representative changes, zero-measure superlevel sets, positive finite thresholds approaching zero, and rejected zero/infinite-threshold encodings.
